questions.question: What incident metrics are most useful?
questions.preferred_answer: Use time to acknowledge, time to restore, recurrence, reopen rate, backlog age, user impact, escalation, handoff count, communication quality, and service-specific reliability. Average resolution time alone can hide severe outliers.

questions.question: A high-priority incident has no clear resolver team. What do you do?
questions.preferred_answer: Assign an accountable coordinator, stabilize impact, bring likely domain owners into a shared channel, use service maps and recent-change data, escalate resource gaps, document decisions, and keep stakeholders updated while ownership is resolved.

questions.question: What qualifies as a major incident?
questions.preferred_answer: A major incident is an incident with exceptional business impact or urgency requiring a distinct coordinated response. Criteria should include critical services, scale, safety, revenue, compliance, public visibility, or strategic events.

questions.question: What is the role of an incident commander?
questions.preferred_answer: The incident commander owns coordination, priorities, decisions, roles, and operational tempo. They create clarity and remove blockers while technical leads investigate and execute. The role should not be overloaded with every task.

questions.question: What roles are useful during a major incident?
questions.preferred_answer: Common roles include incident commander, technical lead, communications lead, scribe, operations liaison, business liaison, and subject-matter responders. Roles can be combined for smaller incidents but responsibilities must remain explicit.

questions.question: Why should technical response and stakeholder communication be separated?
questions.preferred_answer: Responders need uninterrupted diagnostic focus, while stakeholders need regular, translated updates. A communications role prevents engineers from repeating explanations and reduces contradictory messages.

questions.question: What should a major-incident update contain?
questions.preferred_answer: State current impact, affected services or users, start time, response status, workaround, actions underway, decisions or risks, and next update time. Separate confirmed facts from hypotheses and avoid unsupported recovery promises.

questions.question: How often should updates be sent?
questions.preferred_answer: Set a cadence based on severity and stakeholder need, such as every 15 or 30 minutes, and send an update even if there is no material change. Change the cadence transparently as the incident stabilizes.

questions.question: What is a “single source of truth” during an incident?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the authoritative record for impact, timeline, owners, decisions, actions, and communications. Chat can support collaboration, but key facts and decisions must be captured in a durable incident record.

questions.question: Why is a scribe valuable?
questions.preferred_answer: A scribe records timestamps, observations, decisions, actions, owners, and outcomes. This reduces memory errors, supports handovers, enables accurate communication, and provides evidence for review without distracting technical responders.

questions.question: How should hypotheses be managed during an incident?
questions.preferred_answer: Record hypotheses with supporting and contradicting evidence, owner, test, and result. Avoid treating the first plausible explanation as fact. Time-box investigation and prioritize tests that can safely narrow the search space.

questions.question: When is rollback preferred over further debugging?
questions.preferred_answer: Rollback is preferred when a recent change is strongly correlated, rollback is safe and tested, continued impact is material, and the previous state is known to be healthier. Preserve evidence and consider data compatibility before acting.

questions.question: How should executive communication differ from technical communication?
questions.preferred_answer: Executives need business impact, risk, decisions, customer implications, recovery confidence, and resource needs. Technical responders need evidence, topology, logs, commands, and hypotheses. Both must remain factually aligned.

questions.question: What should be included in a post-incident review?
questions.preferred_answer: Include impact, timeline, detection, response, contributing conditions, what helped or hindered, customer communication, action items, owners, due dates, and systemic lessons. Avoid reducing the review to a single human error.

questions.question: What makes an incident review blameless?
questions.preferred_answer: It examines how system conditions, incentives, interfaces, information, workload, and safeguards shaped reasonable actions at the time. Blameless does not mean accountability-free; it means learning without scapegoating.

questions.question: How should action items from incident reviews be prioritized?
questions.preferred_answer: Prioritize by recurrence likelihood, potential impact, risk reduction, effort, dependency, and whether the action improves detection, containment, recovery, or prevention. Track owners and verify effectiveness after completion.

questions.question: When should external parties be notified?
questions.preferred_answer: Follow contractual, regulatory, legal, security, privacy, and customer-communication requirements. Coordinate with authorized functions; do not delay mandatory reporting while waiting for perfect technical certainty.

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.question: A major outage has competing technical leads proposing opposite actions. How do you proceed?
questions.preferred_answer: The incident commander clarifies decision authority, compares evidence, risk, reversibility, and expected recovery time, time-boxes debate, chooses or sequences the safest test, records the decision, and defines rollback criteria.

questions.question: What is a problem in ITSM?
questions.preferred_answer: A problem is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. Problem management reduces the likelihood and impact of incidents by identifying causes, managing workarounds, and initiating permanent improvement.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: How is problem management different from incident management?
questions.preferred_answer: Incident management restores service quickly. Problem management investigates causes and systemic conditions to prevent recurrence or reduce impact. They are connected but have different objectives and time horizons.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is a known error?
questions.preferred_answer: A known error is a problem that has been analyzed but not fully resolved, usually with a documented cause or contributing condition and a workaround. It should remain actively reviewed, not become a permanent excuse.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is reactive problem management?
questions.preferred_answer: Reactive problem management starts after incidents or trends reveal an issue. It uses incident data, technical evidence, and stakeholder impact to identify and address causes or reduce recurrence.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is proactive problem management?
questions.preferred_answer: Proactive problem management identifies weaknesses before major incidents through trend analysis, monitoring, risk assessment, capacity reviews, vendor advisories, technical debt, and recurring near misses.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: When should an incident create a problem record?
questions.preferred_answer: Create one when recurrence, impact, unknown cause, risk, workaround dependency, cross-team pattern, or improvement value justifies structured investigation. Not every incident needs a separate problem record.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is the 5 Whys technique?
questions.preferred_answer: It repeatedly asks why an outcome occurred to move from symptoms toward underlying conditions. It is quick but can oversimplify complex systems, so validate each link with evidence and consider multiple causal paths.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is a fishbone diagram useful for?
questions.preferred_answer: It structures possible contributing factors across categories such as people, process, technology, environment, suppliers, and measurement. It supports broad exploration but does not prove causality.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is Pareto analysis in problem management?
questions.preferred_answer: Pareto analysis ranks categories by frequency or impact to focus effort on the few contributors responsible for much of the loss. Use reliable categorization and avoid ignoring rare but catastrophic risks.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: Why is “human error” an incomplete root cause?
questions.preferred_answer: It describes an action, not why the action was reasonable or possible. A useful analysis examines interface design, training, workload, procedures, access, safeguards, incentives, automation, and detection.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: How should recurring incidents be identified?
questions.preferred_answer: Use normalized categories, affected configuration items, symptom signatures, monitoring events, error codes, timing, recent changes, and text analytics. Validate clusters with technical review because poor ticket data can create false patterns.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is the difference between root cause and contributing factor?
questions.preferred_answer: A root cause is a condition whose removal materially prevents recurrence within the defined scope. Contributing factors increase likelihood or impact. Complex incidents often have several interacting causes rather than one root.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: How should a workaround be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Record prerequisites, risks, steps, validation, ownership, expiry or review date, affected services, and rollback. Train support teams and monitor use so temporary work does not silently become permanent architecture.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: How do you measure problem-management effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Track recurrence and impact reduction, known-error age, time to useful workaround, action completion, risk retired, incidents linked to problems, and verified improvement outcomes - not only the number of records closed.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What should happen when the exact root cause cannot be proven?
questions.preferred_answer: Document evidence, bounded hypotheses, eliminated causes, residual risk, monitoring improvements, mitigations, and follow-up experiments. Do not invent certainty; risk reduction and better detection can still be valuable outcomes.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: A recurring issue is always fixed by restarting a service. What is your next step?
questions.preferred_answer: Treat restart as a workaround, collect pre-restart evidence, correlate resource and dependency behavior, examine leaks or deadlocks, define safe thresholds, create a problem record, and pursue a permanent corrective change.
questions.category: 5. Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis

questions.question: What is the objective of change enablement?
questions.preferred_answer: To maximize successful service and product changes by assessing risk, authorizing appropriate changes, and managing schedules while enabling useful change at the required speed.

questions.question: What is a standard change?
questions.preferred_answer: A standard change is low risk, well understood, documented, repeatable, and pre-authorized. It still requires defined criteria, controls, evidence, and periodic review; it is not an untracked change.

questions.question: What is a normal change?
questions.preferred_answer: A normal change requires assessment and authorization appropriate to its risk, impact, complexity, and timing. The workflow should be proportionate rather than applying the same approval depth to every change.

questions.question: What is an emergency change?
questions.preferred_answer: An emergency change is expedited because delay would cause unacceptable harm, such as restoring a major service or addressing a critical vulnerability. It requires defined authority, minimum safe evidence, retrospective review, and documentation.

questions.question: How should change risk be assessed?
questions.preferred_answer: Consider service criticality, blast radius, novelty, reversibility, data impact, security, dependencies, timing, test evidence, operator experience, failure history, observability, and fallback readiness. Use data but preserve expert judgment.

questions.question: What should a change record contain?
questions.preferred_answer: Purpose, affected services and configuration items, owner, implementation plan, test evidence, risk, impact, dependencies, schedule, communications, approvals, validation, rollback criteria, and post-implementation result.

questions.question: What is a change advisory board (CAB) for?
questions.preferred_answer: A CAB supports assessment, coordination, and authorization of changes that need cross-functional judgment. It should focus on material risk and conflicts, not act as a weekly approval queue for every routine deployment.

questions.question: How can organizations reduce CAB bottlenecks?
questions.preferred_answer: Pre-authorize safe patterns, automate policy checks and evidence, use risk-based routing, schedule asynchronous review, define clear decision rights, and reserve meetings for complex or conflicting changes.

questions.question: What is a change freeze?
questions.preferred_answer: A change freeze restricts specified changes during sensitive periods. It should define scope, dates, exceptions, authority, and emergency handling. Blanket freezes can defer risk and create a dangerous post-freeze backlog.

questions.question: What is a rollback plan?
questions.preferred_answer: A rollback plan describes how to return to a known safe state, including triggers, data compatibility, timing, permissions, backups, communications, and validation. “Restore backup” is not a complete rollback plan.

questions.question: What is the difference between release and deployment?
questions.preferred_answer: Deployment moves a component or version into an environment. Release makes functionality available for use. Feature flags and staged rollout can separate these events to reduce risk.

questions.question: What is a canary deployment?
questions.preferred_answer: A canary exposes a change to a small controlled population, monitors agreed health and business metrics, and expands only if results are acceptable. It requires representative traffic, observability, and automated halt or rollback criteria.

source.title: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework - Operational Excellence

questions.question: What is a blue-green deployment?
questions.preferred_answer: Blue-green maintains two production-capable environments and switches traffic from the current to the new version after validation. It speeds rollback but adds cost and requires careful data and session compatibility.

questions.question: How should failed changes be reviewed?
questions.preferred_answer: Assess planning, assumptions, testing, dependencies, observability, execution, decisions, and recovery without scapegoating. Update risk models, standard patterns, automation, and training based on evidence.

questions.question: Which metrics indicate healthy change performance?
questions.preferred_answer: Use deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, failed-deployment recovery time, unauthorized changes, rollback effectiveness, and service impact. Balance speed, stability, and value rather than optimizing one metric.

questions.question: A security patch is urgent but the rollback is uncertain. How do you decide?
questions.preferred_answer: Compare exploit and business risk with change risk, reduce scope, test representative paths, create backups or snapshots, define containment, involve security and service owners, document authority, and monitor closely after implementation.

questions.question: What is service request management?
questions.preferred_answer: It handles predefined, user-initiated requests in an effective and user-friendly way, such as information, access, standard equipment, or routine service actions. It should be designed for predictable fulfillment and transparency.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What belongs in a service catalog entry?
questions.preferred_answer: Include purpose, eligibility, request inputs, approvals, fulfillment steps, target times, support, cost or charge, dependencies, security classification, and expected outcome in language users understand.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How should request forms be designed?
questions.preferred_answer: Ask only for information required for decision or fulfillment, use conditional fields, plain language, defaults, validation, and visible expectations. Excessive mandatory fields drive poor data and shadow channels.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is request fulfillment automation suitable for?
questions.preferred_answer: Automate stable, high-volume, rules-based requests with reliable data, controlled permissions, exception handling, audit trails, and rollback. Human review remains necessary for ambiguity, sensitive access, and material risk.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How is access management connected to identity governance?
questions.preferred_answer: Access management executes authorized access, while identity governance defines policies, ownership, lifecycle, certification, segregation of duties, and accountability. Requests should use authoritative identity and role data.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is least privilege?
questions.preferred_answer: Grant only the access needed for a defined role and duration, with appropriate review and removal. Least privilege applies to users, service accounts, automation, APIs, and administrators.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is segregation of duties?
questions.preferred_answer: It separates conflicting responsibilities so one person cannot complete a high-risk transaction or bypass controls alone. Exceptions should be documented, time-bound, approved, monitored, and reviewed.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How should joiner-mover-leaver access be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Use authoritative HR or identity events, role-based access, timely provisioning and removal, approval evidence, exception handling, reconciliation, and periodic review. Movers are often the largest source of accumulated excess access.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What makes a knowledge article effective?
questions.preferred_answer: It is findable, accurate, scoped, actionable, safe, written for its audience, versioned, owned, and validated through use. Include symptoms, prerequisites, steps, expected results, escalation, and review date.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is knowledge-centered service (KCS) trying to achieve?
questions.preferred_answer: It integrates knowledge creation and improvement into support work so solutions are captured in the workflow, reused, reviewed, and improved based on demand. The goal is collective learning, not merely article counts.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How do you measure self-service quality?
questions.preferred_answer: Measure successful completion, search success, deflection with verified outcome, time and effort, abandonment, escalation, article helpfulness, and repeat demand. Deflection alone can hide users who gave up.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: When should a knowledge article be retired?
questions.preferred_answer: Retire or archive when the service, interface, control, or workaround is obsolete; the content is duplicated; risk has changed; or usage and feedback show it no longer helps. Preserve required historical records separately.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How can request categories become harmful?
questions.preferred_answer: Too many categories confuse users and agents, fragment reporting, and create routing errors. Design around user intent and fulfillment ownership, then maintain a normalized taxonomy behind the interface.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: How should privileged access requests differ from ordinary requests?
questions.preferred_answer: Require stronger identity verification, explicit business justification, least privilege, defined duration, elevated approval, secure delivery, session or activity logging, emergency paths, and timely revocation.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is a request model?
questions.preferred_answer: A request model defines the repeatable workflow, roles, approvals, automation, target times, controls, communications, and fulfillment evidence for a known request type.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: Users bypass the portal and message engineers directly. How do you respond?
questions.preferred_answer: Investigate friction, urgency, trust, and catalog gaps; simplify entry; integrate channels where appropriate; make status visible; protect urgent paths; and coach teams not to reward bypassing with invisible work.
questions.category: 7. Service Requests, Access, and Knowledge Management

questions.question: What is the purpose of a service desk?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the entry point and communication interface between provider and users, capturing demand, resolving issues, coordinating support, sharing knowledge, and representing the user experience across services.

questions.question: What skills matter beyond technical knowledge at a service desk?
questions.preferred_answer: Active listening, structured questioning, empathy, concise writing, expectation setting, ownership, prioritization, security awareness, cultural sensitivity, and knowing when to escalate are essential.

questions.question: What is first-contact resolution?
questions.preferred_answer: FCR is the proportion of contacts resolved during the initial interaction without transfer or follow-up. It is useful only when resolution quality, recurrence, user effort, and appropriate escalation are also monitored.

questions.question: How should an agent clarify a vague issue?
questions.preferred_answer: Confirm the desired outcome, exact symptom, start time, scope, affected device or service, recent change, error message, reproduction steps, impact, and what has already been tried. Summarize understanding before acting.

questions.question: How do you communicate with a frustrated user?
questions.preferred_answer: Acknowledge impact, avoid defensiveness, clarify facts, state ownership and next actions, give realistic timing, provide updates, and explain constraints plainly. Empathy should accompany useful action rather than replace it.

questions.question: What is customer effort, and why measure it?
questions.preferred_answer: Customer effort reflects how difficult it is to obtain help or complete a service interaction. High effort predicts dissatisfaction even when the ticket closes, and often reveals poor forms, handoffs, authentication, or status visibility.

questions.question: How should remote troubleshooting be performed safely?
questions.preferred_answer: Confirm identity and consent, explain actions, protect sensitive information, use approved tools, preserve user work, avoid unnecessary privilege, document changes, verify the outcome, and disconnect securely.

questions.question: What makes a warm transfer different from a cold transfer?
questions.preferred_answer: A warm transfer briefs the receiving team, confirms acceptance, and sets expectations for the user. A cold transfer sends the user or ticket onward without context, increasing effort and repeat explanation.

questions.question: How should ticket categorization be balanced with speed?
questions.preferred_answer: Capture the minimum accurate category needed for routing and analysis, use defaults or automation, and allow correction later. Do not delay urgent restoration for perfect taxonomy.

questions.question: What is shift-left support?
questions.preferred_answer: Shift-left moves suitable knowledge, access, diagnostics, and resolution capability closer to users or front-line teams. It must include training, guardrails, tooling, feedback, and escalation - not simply transfer workload downward.

questions.question: What is shift-right in operations?
questions.preferred_answer: Shift-right brings operational learning, observability, resilience testing, and user behavior from production back into design and delivery. It helps teams build services that are easier to operate and support.

questions.question: How should VIP support be handled without damaging fairness?
questions.preferred_answer: Define transparent service tiers or business-critical criteria, avoid informal favoritism, protect security controls, and ensure ordinary users still receive agreed service. Escalation should be based on impact and commitments.

questions.question: What is the risk of measuring agents mainly by handle time?
questions.preferred_answer: Agents may rush diagnosis, avoid complex work, create repeat contacts, or transfer prematurely. Balance efficiency with quality, first-contact resolution, recurrence, customer effort, compliance, and coaching.

questions.question: How do you improve escalation quality?
questions.preferred_answer: Define entry criteria, required evidence, ownership, severity, actions tried, logs, time sensitivity, and next decision needed. Review rejected or bounced escalations to improve knowledge and routing.

questions.question: What is a support swarming model?
questions.preferred_answer: Swarming brings relevant expertise to the issue without repeatedly transferring ownership through tiers. It can improve learning and resolution but needs clear coordination, availability, and documentation.

questions.question: An agent repeatedly meets SLA by closing tickets that reopen. How do you address it?
questions.preferred_answer: Review incentives and definitions, coach on validation and documentation, track reopen and recurrence, sample quality, correct the metric, and handle intentional manipulation through normal performance and governance processes.

questions.question: What is a service level agreement (SLA)?
questions.preferred_answer: An SLA documents agreed service targets, scope, responsibilities, measurement rules, exclusions, reporting, and review between provider and customer. It should reflect meaningful outcomes rather than only internal activity.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is an operational level agreement (OLA)?
questions.preferred_answer: An OLA defines internal commitments between teams that support delivery of an external service level. It aligns handoffs, responsibilities, and targets without exposing every internal metric to the customer.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: How does an underpinning contract relate to an SLA?
questions.preferred_answer: A supplier contract supports provider commitments through service, support, security, continuity, and performance obligations. Supplier targets should align with the end-to-end service promise and leave room for internal processing.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is an SLO?
questions.preferred_answer: A service level objective is a measurable reliability target for a service indicator, such as successful request rate or latency. SLOs help teams balance reliability and delivery decisions.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is an SLI?
questions.preferred_answer: A service level indicator is a quantitative measure of service behavior experienced by users, such as availability, latency, throughput, correctness, or freshness. It should be defined from a clear measurement point.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is an error budget?
questions.preferred_answer: An error budget is the allowed unreliability implied by an SLO. Teams use its consumption to guide risk, release pace, reliability work, and escalation, rather than treating 100 percent reliability as a universal goal.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: Why can percentage availability be misleading?
questions.preferred_answer: The same percentage can hide duration, frequency, affected users, partial degradation, business timing, and dependency failures. Define calculation, exclusions, measurement point, and customer impact clearly.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What makes a KPI useful?
questions.preferred_answer: A KPI connects to an objective, has a clear definition, owner, data source, target, review cadence, and decision use. It should be hard to game and balanced with counter-metrics.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is the difference between leading and lagging indicators?
questions.preferred_answer: Leading indicators signal conditions that may influence future outcomes, such as alert noise or change-risk scores. Lagging indicators report results already experienced, such as outage minutes. Both are needed.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: How should SLA clocks handle waiting for users?
questions.preferred_answer: Define pause conditions transparently, record when and why the clock pauses, send reminders, and avoid using pauses to hide provider delay. Customer-facing elapsed time may still be reported separately from contractual time.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is the danger of using averages alone?
questions.preferred_answer: Averages hide distribution, severe outliers, priority mix, and different user groups. Use percentiles, ranges, volumes, age bands, and service segmentation alongside averages.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What should an operations dashboard emphasize?
questions.preferred_answer: Show service health, customer impact, current risk, significant trends, actionable exceptions, ownership, and decision context. Avoid dense counts that do not indicate what action is needed.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

source.title: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework - Operational Excellence

questions.question: How should backlog health be measured?
questions.preferred_answer: Measure volume by age, priority, service, ownership, waiting reason, breaches, inflow versus outflow, and repeat demand. A stable total can hide an aging high-risk subset.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is experience-level measurement?
questions.preferred_answer: It evaluates how users perceive and accomplish outcomes, such as task success, effort, responsiveness, and confidence. It complements technical and process metrics rather than replacing them.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: How do you prevent metric gaming?
questions.preferred_answer: Use balanced measures, clear intent, quality sampling, outcome checks, transparent definitions, segmentation, audit trails, and regular review of unintended behavior. Do not tie one narrow metric directly to rewards.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: An SLA is consistently met, but users remain dissatisfied. What do you investigate?
questions.preferred_answer: Review whether targets reflect user priorities, measurement starts and stops, partial degradation, effort, communication, recurrence, resolution quality, and underserved segments. Revise the service-level model using customer evidence.
questions.category: 9. Service Levels, Metrics, Reporting, and Experience

questions.question: What is an event in IT operations?
questions.preferred_answer: An event is a change of state significant for managing a service or configuration item. Events can be informational, warning, or exception conditions and may or may not require human action.

questions.question: How is an event different from an alert?
questions.preferred_answer: An event is observed state information. An alert is a notification that a condition likely requires attention based on rules, correlation, or analysis. Not every event should produce an alert.

questions.question: What is observability?
questions.preferred_answer: Observability is the ability to understand a system’s internal state from its external outputs and telemetry. It supports investigation of novel failures, not only predefined threshold monitoring.

questions.question: What are the main telemetry signals?
questions.preferred_answer: Metrics summarize numerical behavior, logs record discrete events, traces follow requests across components, and profiles describe resource use. Context and correlation across signals are more valuable than collecting everything.

questions.question: What makes an alert actionable?
questions.preferred_answer: It identifies a meaningful symptom, affected service, severity, evidence, owner, urgency, likely next action, and runbook. It should fire early enough to act but not for conditions requiring no response.

questions.question: What is alert fatigue?
questions.preferred_answer: Alert fatigue occurs when excessive, repetitive, low-value, or unactionable notifications reduce attention and response quality. Reduce it through ownership, deduplication, tuning, automation, and removal of unused alerts.

questions.question: What is the difference between symptom-based and cause-based alerts?
questions.preferred_answer: Symptom alerts reflect user-visible failure and are often best for paging. Cause alerts identify internal conditions and may support diagnosis. Paging on every possible cause creates noise and misses novel failure modes.

questions.question: Why use percentiles for latency?
questions.preferred_answer: Percentiles reveal tail behavior experienced by slower requests, which averages can hide. Choose percentiles and windows based on service expectations, volume, and user impact.

questions.question: What is event correlation?
questions.preferred_answer: Event correlation groups related signals using time, topology, dependency, signature, and causal context to reduce duplicates and identify likely incidents. Correlation logic must be tested to avoid suppressing important evidence.

questions.question: What is a heartbeat or synthetic check?
questions.preferred_answer: A heartbeat confirms a component can report; a synthetic check actively executes a user-like path. Both can detect failures, but neither alone proves full end-to-end service health.

questions.question: How should monitoring ownership be assigned?
questions.preferred_answer: Every alert, dashboard, data pipeline, and runbook should have an owner responsible for quality, response, maintenance, and retirement. Unowned monitoring inevitably becomes stale.

questions.question: What retention considerations apply to logs?
questions.preferred_answer: Balance investigation, legal, audit, privacy, cost, and operational needs. Define classification, access, integrity, retention, deletion, and secure transfer; do not retain sensitive logs indefinitely by default.

source.title: NIST SP 800-92 - Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: What is cardinality, and why does it matter for metrics?
questions.preferred_answer: Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations. Unbounded values such as user IDs or request IDs can increase cost and degrade monitoring systems. Use logs or traces for high-cardinality detail where appropriate.

questions.question: How do you validate a new alert?
questions.preferred_answer: Test normal and failure conditions, threshold and window behavior, routing, deduplication, runbook accuracy, permissions, recovery notification, and expected operator action. Review its value after real use.

questions.question: What is telemetry sampling?
questions.preferred_answer: Sampling retains a subset of traces, events, or profiles to control volume and cost. Strategies should preserve errors, rare events, important transactions, and enough unbiased data for analysis.

questions.question: A dashboard is green while customers report failure. What do you do?
questions.preferred_answer: Treat customer evidence as a signal, verify the critical user journey, check measurement points and stale data, compare dependencies and regions, inspect recent changes, and add missing service-level telemetry after restoration.

questions.question: What is a configuration item (CI)?
questions.preferred_answer: A CI is a component that must be managed to deliver a service, such as an application, server, database, document, supplier service, or business capability. Its attributes and relationships depend on management needs.

questions.question: What is a CMDB?
questions.preferred_answer: A configuration management database stores information about CIs and their relationships to support impact analysis, incident response, change, compliance, and service management. It is not automatically trustworthy merely because data exists.

questions.question: How is asset management different from configuration management?
questions.preferred_answer: Asset management focuses on financial, contractual, ownership, lifecycle, and compliance value. Configuration management focuses on attributes and relationships needed to manage services. The same item can be both an asset and a CI.

questions.question: What makes CMDB scope manageable?
questions.preferred_answer: Start with clear use cases and critical services, define required CI classes and attributes, owners, sources, reconciliation, and quality measures. Expanding without purpose creates expensive low-trust data.

questions.question: What is service mapping?
questions.preferred_answer: Service mapping represents dependencies between business services and supporting applications, infrastructure, data, networks, teams, and suppliers. It supports impact analysis but requires ongoing validation.

questions.question: What is discovery in configuration management?
questions.preferred_answer: Discovery uses agents, APIs, network scans, cloud inventories, or integrations to detect technical components and attributes. It cannot reliably infer every business relationship, ownership, or criticality without governance.

questions.question: What is reconciliation?
questions.preferred_answer: Reconciliation resolves conflicts when multiple sources update the same CI attributes. Rules define source authority, precedence, identity matching, timestamps, and exception handling.

questions.question: How is CMDB data quality measured?
questions.preferred_answer: Measure completeness, correctness, currency, uniqueness, consistency, relationship integrity, ownership, and usefulness for target processes. Sample against authoritative evidence rather than relying only on database constraints.

questions.question: Why are CI relationships important?
questions.preferred_answer: Relationships reveal blast radius, upstream and downstream dependencies, ownership, and recovery order. A flat inventory cannot support reliable service-impact analysis.

questions.question: What is a system of record?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the authoritative source for a defined data element or domain. CMDB design should identify authoritative sources rather than allowing every tool to overwrite shared attributes.

questions.question: What is software asset management?
questions.preferred_answer: It manages software entitlement, deployment, usage, cost, compliance, risk, and lifecycle. Effective SAM requires reliable inventory, contract interpretation, normalization, reclamation, and controlled procurement.

questions.question: How should cloud resources be identified and owned?
questions.preferred_answer: Use mandatory metadata or tags, account and subscription structure, automated policy, cost allocation, owner and service mapping, expiration for temporary assets, and reconciliation with cloud inventory APIs.

questions.question: What should happen when an asset is retired?
questions.preferred_answer: Remove access, sanitize data, update inventory and relationships, terminate licenses and support, handle records and disposal securely, validate dependencies, and retain required evidence.

questions.question: Why does a CMDB often lose trust?
questions.preferred_answer: Common causes are unclear use cases, too much scope, conflicting sources, poor ownership, manual updates, stale relationships, and dashboards that reward record count rather than correctness.

questions.question: How should unauthorized configuration drift be handled?
questions.preferred_answer: Detect and classify drift, determine whether it is legitimate or risky, preserve evidence, restore or approve the state through controlled change, and improve automation or access controls to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: During an outage the CMDB is clearly outdated. How do you use it?
questions.preferred_answer: Treat it as one hypothesis source, verify dependencies with telemetry, cloud inventories, architecture records, and responders, document discrepancies, and create owned corrections after the incident rather than trusting or discarding it wholesale.

questions.question: What is availability management?
questions.preferred_answer: It ensures services deliver agreed availability by understanding requirements, designing resilience, measuring user experience, analyzing failures, and improving components and operational practices.

questions.question: How is reliability different from availability?
questions.preferred_answer: Availability concerns whether a service is usable when needed. Reliability concerns consistent failure-free behavior over time. A service may be frequently available but unreliable if it repeatedly degrades or fails briefly.

questions.question: What is capacity management?
questions.preferred_answer: Capacity management ensures services and resources can meet current and future demand at appropriate performance and cost. It combines business demand, service behavior, component usage, and forecasting.

questions.question: What is demand management?
questions.preferred_answer: Demand management understands and influences patterns of business activity and service consumption. It supports capacity, scheduling, pricing, throttling, and user communication without simply suppressing legitimate demand.

questions.question: What is an RTO?
questions.preferred_answer: Recovery time objective is the target duration for restoring a service or capability after disruption. It informs architecture, staffing, procedures, suppliers, and testing.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is an RPO?
questions.preferred_answer: Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. It drives backup, replication, journaling, and recovery design and should be set by business impact.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is a business impact analysis?
questions.preferred_answer: A BIA identifies critical processes, dependencies, impacts over time, maximum tolerable disruption, recovery priorities, resource needs, and legal or contractual requirements. It provides the basis for continuity strategies.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is a single point of failure?
questions.preferred_answer: It is a component, dependency, person, supplier, or process whose failure can interrupt the service without an effective alternative. Redundancy must be independent and tested to remove the actual failure mode.

questions.question: What is graceful degradation?
questions.preferred_answer: Graceful degradation preserves the most important service capabilities when resources or dependencies fail, instead of complete outage. It requires prioritization, isolation, fallback behavior, and user communication.

questions.question: What is load shedding?
questions.preferred_answer: Load shedding deliberately rejects or defers lower-priority work to protect essential service under overload. It needs fair policy, visible errors, retry control, monitoring, and recovery criteria.

questions.question: How should capacity thresholds be selected?
questions.preferred_answer: Use performance tests, growth trends, lead time, saturation behavior, failover needs, seasonality, and business forecasts. Static percentages without context can alert too early or too late.

source.title: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework - Operational Excellence

questions.question: What is resilience testing?
questions.preferred_answer: It deliberately validates recovery, failover, dependency behavior, and operational response under controlled faults or disruption. Start safely, define hypotheses and abort conditions, and learn from results.

questions.question: Why must backups be restored in tests?
questions.preferred_answer: A successful backup job proves only that data was written. Restore testing validates readability, completeness, credentials, dependencies, timing, procedure, and whether recovery objectives can actually be met.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What should a continuity plan include?
questions.preferred_answer: Scope, activation criteria, roles, contacts, dependencies, alternate arrangements, recovery steps, communications, security, data recovery, supplier actions, validation, return to normal, and exercise schedule.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: How should capacity and cost be balanced in cloud services?
questions.preferred_answer: Use service objectives, autoscaling, reservations or commitments where justified, rightsizing, demand shaping, budgets, unit economics, and resilience requirements. Cost reduction must not silently remove recovery margin.

questions.question: A failover test succeeds technically but exceeds the RTO. What next?
questions.preferred_answer: Measure where time was spent, automate or parallelize safe steps, improve detection and decision authority, pre-stage access, reduce dependency recovery time, revise architecture or the business target, and retest end to end.

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is a runbook?
questions.preferred_answer: A runbook is an operational procedure for a recurring task or response, including purpose, prerequisites, steps, decision points, validation, rollback, escalation, owner, and review information.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: How is a playbook different from a runbook?
questions.preferred_answer: Usage varies, but a runbook usually gives task-level operational steps, while a playbook coordinates broader response patterns, roles, and choices for a scenario. Organizations should define their terminology.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What makes a procedure safe to automate?
questions.preferred_answer: It has clear inputs, stable rules, reliable data, bounded scope, permissions, idempotency or safe retry, validation, logging, exception handling, rollback, ownership, and testing.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What is idempotent automation?
questions.preferred_answer: Running it more than once produces the intended state without duplicate harmful effects. Idempotency supports retries and recovery but still requires concurrency control and audit evidence.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: Why should automation use least privilege?
questions.preferred_answer: Automation can act quickly and at scale. Restricting permissions, scope, duration, and secrets limits blast radius if logic, credentials, or inputs fail.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What should an operational handover contain?
questions.preferred_answer: Current service health, active incidents, risky changes, pending work, capacity or certificate concerns, external dependencies, decisions, stakeholder commitments, and explicit ownership. Handover should be acknowledged.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: How should scheduled jobs be monitored?
questions.preferred_answer: Monitor start, completion, duration, outcome, data freshness, dependencies, retries, and business impact. Distinguish “job ran” from “expected result was produced.”
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What is operational readiness review?
questions.preferred_answer: It evaluates whether a new or changed service can be operated safely: monitoring, support model, runbooks, access, capacity, security, continuity, ownership, documentation, training, and known risks.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

source.title: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework - Operational Excellence

questions.question: What is toil in SRE?
questions.preferred_answer: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work that scales with service growth and has limited enduring value. Some operational work is necessary; toil should be measured and reduced deliberately.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: How should automation opportunities be prioritized?
questions.preferred_answer: Prioritize by volume, time, error rate, risk reduction, scalability, user delay, standardization, and maintenance cost. Do not automate rare ambiguous work solely because it is disliked.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What is a control room or NOC operating rhythm?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the recurring cadence for health review, alerts, incidents, changes, capacity, handovers, escalation, and reporting. The rhythm should support decisions, not become repetitive meetings without action.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: Why should manual emergency actions be rehearsed?
questions.preferred_answer: During severe failure, normal tools or automation may be unavailable. Rehearsal validates access, knowledge, communications, timing, and safeguards under stress.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

source.title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.question: What is a maintenance window?
questions.preferred_answer: A maintenance window is an agreed period for planned operational work, with scope, communication, risk, service expectations, validation, and contingency. It does not remove the need for change control.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: How should secrets be handled in scripts and runbooks?
questions.preferred_answer: Use managed secret stores, short-lived credentials, least privilege, rotation, access logging, and redaction. Never embed reusable passwords or tokens in code, tickets, or documentation.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: How do you validate an automated remediation?
questions.preferred_answer: Test trigger accuracy, scope, concurrency, failure modes, audit logs, rollback, rate limits, user impact, and whether it masks a deeper problem. Start in limited mode and review outcomes.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: An automation repeatedly fixes an alert but the alert returns daily. What do you do?
questions.preferred_answer: Keep the safe mitigation if needed, create problem work, collect pre-action evidence, analyze recurrence, review whether automation hides impact, set ownership and expiry, and pursue a permanent correction.
questions.category: 13. Operational Procedures, Runbooks, Automation, and Shift Management

questions.question: What is IT governance?
questions.preferred_answer: IT governance evaluates stakeholder needs, sets direction and policy, and monitors performance, risk, and compliance so technology supports enterprise objectives. It clarifies decision rights and accountability.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is risk in an operational context?
questions.preferred_answer: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, often assessed through likelihood, impact, exposure, controls, and residual risk. Operational decisions should consider business, security, safety, compliance, and service risk.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is a risk register?
questions.preferred_answer: A risk register records risk statements, causes, consequences, owners, likelihood, impact, controls, treatment, residual risk, due dates, and review status. It supports decisions; it should not become a static compliance list.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is a control owner?
questions.preferred_answer: A control owner is accountable for the control design, operation, evidence, testing, exceptions, and improvement. Execution may be delegated, but accountability should remain clear.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is residual risk?
questions.preferred_answer: Residual risk remains after controls and treatments are applied. It must be evaluated against risk appetite and explicitly accepted, further treated, transferred, or avoided by authorized owners.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: How should operational teams support audits?
questions.preferred_answer: Maintain accurate evidence through normal workflows, understand control purpose, provide scoped records, explain exceptions, protect sensitive data, and remediate findings based on risk rather than creating last-minute documents.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is evidence integrity?
questions.preferred_answer: Evidence must be complete, accurate, attributable, time-stamped, protected from unauthorized alteration, retained appropriately, and reproducible enough to support review. Screenshots alone may be weak evidence.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

source.title: NIST SP 800-92 - Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: How is a security incident different from an ordinary IT incident?
questions.preferred_answer: A security incident involves actual or suspected compromise of confidentiality, integrity, availability, policy, or control and may require evidence preservation, containment, legal, privacy, and regulatory actions beyond normal restoration.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.question: What are the main phases of incident response?
questions.preferred_answer: Common phases include preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication, and recovery; and post-incident activity. Organizations adapt them to risk, legal duties, and operating model.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.question: Why is chain of custody important?
questions.preferred_answer: It documents who collected, handled, transferred, stored, and analyzed evidence so integrity and admissibility can be assessed. Operational teams should follow authorized forensic procedures rather than improvising.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

source.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.question: What is data minimization in operations?
questions.preferred_answer: Collect, display, retain, and share only data necessary for the operational purpose. Logs, tickets, screenshots, and monitoring can expose personal or sensitive information and need classification and access control.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: How should policy exceptions be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Document business justification, scope, owner, risk assessment, compensating controls, approval, expiry, monitoring, and review. Permanent exceptions should trigger policy or architecture reassessment.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is segregation between development and production access meant to achieve?
questions.preferred_answer: It reduces unauthorized or unreviewed production change and protects data and evidence. Practical models may use just-in-time access, approvals, logging, peer review, and emergency break-glass paths.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: What is a break-glass process?
questions.preferred_answer: It provides emergency privileged access when normal paths are too slow or unavailable, with strong authentication, limited scope and time, logging, notification, and mandatory retrospective review.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: How do compliance and reliability reinforce each other?
questions.preferred_answer: Clear ownership, controlled change, backups, access management, logging, testing, and incident learning support both reliable services and auditable controls. Compliance should codify useful risk management rather than replace engineering judgment.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: An auditor requests broad production logs containing personal data. What do you do?
questions.preferred_answer: Clarify control objective and scope, involve data and security owners, provide least-necessary evidence through approved secure channels, redact or filter where possible, record access, and preserve audit independence.
questions.category: 14. Governance, Risk, Security, Compliance, and Audit

questions.question: How does ITSM complement DevOps?
questions.preferred_answer: ITSM provides service context, governance, support, risk, and continual improvement; DevOps improves flow, collaboration, automation, and feedback. Effective organizations integrate them rather than treating one as slow control and the other as uncontrolled speed.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is shared ownership in operations?
questions.preferred_answer: Teams that build, run, support, secure, and use a service share responsibility for outcomes. Shared ownership still needs explicit roles, escalation, and decision authority.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What do DORA metrics measure?
questions.preferred_answer: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and failed-deployment recovery time describe software delivery performance. They should be used for learning and system improvement, not ranking individuals.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is “you build it, you run it”?
questions.preferred_answer: It means delivery teams retain meaningful operational responsibility, improving feedback and operability. It requires sustainable on-call, platform support, standards, and product ownership - not simply shifting all support burden to developers.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is an error budget policy?
questions.preferred_answer: It defines how reliability performance affects release and engineering decisions, such as slowing risky changes when the budget is exhausted and prioritizing reliability work. It should be agreed before conflict occurs.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: How does Agile influence service management?
questions.preferred_answer: Agile encourages iterative delivery, customer collaboration, feedback, and adaptation. Service-management controls can be embedded into small increments and automated workflows rather than added as a final gate.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is the role of operations in a Scrum team?
questions.preferred_answer: Scrum does not prescribe an operations role. Operational capabilities, reliability work, support, and nonfunctional requirements should be represented in the product goal, backlog, definition of done, team skills, and stakeholder collaboration.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is platform engineering?
questions.preferred_answer: Platform engineering builds reusable internal capabilities and paved paths that help teams deliver and operate services safely with lower cognitive load. A platform is treated as a product with users and measured outcomes.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is a paved road or golden path?
questions.preferred_answer: It is a supported, secure, observable, and automated way to perform common delivery and operational tasks. Teams can deviate when justified, but the default path makes the safe approach easier.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: How do feature flags support operations?
questions.preferred_answer: They separate deployment from release, enable staged exposure, rapid disablement, and experimentation. Flags need ownership, security, observability, expiry, and testing to avoid permanent complexity.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is observability-driven development?
questions.preferred_answer: Teams design telemetry, service indicators, trace context, logs, and diagnostics as part of the service rather than adding them after failure. Operational acceptance includes whether behavior can be understood.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: How should nonfunctional requirements be handled?
questions.preferred_answer: Translate availability, latency, capacity, security, maintainability, supportability, and recovery needs into measurable acceptance criteria, architecture, tests, and operational readiness - not a generic checklist.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

source.title: Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework - Operational Excellence

questions.question: What is technical debt from an operations perspective?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the future operational cost and risk created by expedient design, manual work, weak observability, unsupported components, or deferred maintenance. Make it visible through incidents, toil, lead time, and risk.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: How can change controls be implemented in CI/CD?
questions.preferred_answer: Encode tests, policy checks, approvals by risk, artifact integrity, segregation, deployment evidence, progressive delivery, monitoring, and rollback in the pipeline. Manual approval should be reserved for decisions requiring judgment.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is a production readiness checklist useful for?
questions.preferred_answer: It ensures ownership, SLOs, monitoring, runbooks, capacity, security, backups, dependencies, support, and failure modes are considered before launch. It should guide discussion and evidence, not become a checkbox ritual.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: A product team deploys frequently but operations sees rising incidents. How do you respond?
questions.preferred_answer: Analyze change-failure patterns and service impact jointly, improve automated tests and progressive delivery, define SLOs and error-budget policy, strengthen operability, and avoid solving the issue with blanket release freezes.
questions.category: 15. Agile, DevOps, SRE, and Product Integration

questions.question: What is the continual improvement model used for?
questions.preferred_answer: It guides improvement by clarifying vision, current state, target state, actions, execution, measurement, and sustained momentum. Teams should revisit assumptions as evidence changes.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How should improvement opportunities be prioritized?
questions.preferred_answer: Use expected value, risk reduction, customer impact, urgency, effort, dependencies, strategic alignment, evidence quality, and ability to learn. Maintain a balanced portfolio of quick wins and structural work.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is process mapping useful for?
questions.preferred_answer: It makes steps, decisions, roles, handoffs, data, controls, queues, and exceptions visible. Validate the map with people doing the work and real cases rather than documenting an idealized flow.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is value-stream mapping?
questions.preferred_answer: It analyzes end-to-end flow from demand to outcome, including wait time, work time, rework, information, and constraints. It helps target system-level improvements instead of local speedups.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How do you identify a process bottleneck?
questions.preferred_answer: Use flow data, queue age, work-in-progress, handoffs, rework, capacity, and observation. The visible slow step may be constrained by policy, information, or upstream variability rather than staffing alone.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is the difference between efficiency and effectiveness?
questions.preferred_answer: Efficiency uses fewer resources for an activity; effectiveness achieves the intended outcome. A faster process that resolves the wrong demand or increases recurrence is efficient but ineffective.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How should standard operating procedures be governed?
questions.preferred_answer: Assign owner, scope, version, approval, effective date, review cycle, change history, training, access, and retirement. Validate that actual work matches the procedure and update either when justified.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is supplier management?
questions.preferred_answer: It ensures suppliers and their performance support service quality, continuity, security, cost, and strategic needs through selection, contracts, relationships, monitoring, risk, and improvement.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What should be reviewed in a supplier service review?
questions.preferred_answer: Service levels, incidents, recurring problems, changes, security, continuity, capacity, costs, risks, obligations, improvement actions, roadmap, and relationship issues. Validate supplier metrics against end-to-end experience.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How should multi-supplier incidents be managed?
questions.preferred_answer: Maintain one service-level coordinator, shared impact and timeline, clear responsibilities, evidence exchange, contractual escalation, and customer communication. Do not make the customer arbitrate supplier boundaries.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is FinOps?
questions.preferred_answer: FinOps is an operational framework and culture that brings engineering, finance, and business together to maximize business value from cloud spending through visibility, accountability, optimization, and iterative decisions.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is unit cost in IT services?
questions.preferred_answer: Unit cost relates service cost to a meaningful output or outcome, such as cost per transaction, user, device, or workload. It helps explain demand, efficiency, and trade-offs better than total spend alone.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How should a process change be introduced?
questions.preferred_answer: Define the problem and outcome, involve affected people, test with a limited group, update roles and tools, train, communicate, measure behavior and results, handle exceptions, and iterate.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: What is psychological safety in incident and improvement work?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the ability to raise risks, admit uncertainty, report mistakes, and challenge decisions without fear of humiliation or retaliation. It improves detection and learning but still includes respectful accountability.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: How should leaders respond to repeated process noncompliance?
questions.preferred_answer: Determine whether the process is understood, practical, supported by tools, aligned with incentives, and proportionate to risk. Fix system barriers, coach behavior, handle deliberate violations fairly, and monitor outcomes.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

questions.question: A vendor meets contractual SLA but causes recurring business disruption. What do you do?
questions.preferred_answer: Present end-to-end impact evidence, review whether contractual measures are fit, open problem and improvement actions, strengthen monitoring and escalation, renegotiate obligations if needed, and maintain contingency or exit options.
questions.category: 16. Continual Improvement, Leadership, Suppliers, and Financial Management

practical_scenarios.title: Payroll service unavailable before salary cutoff
practical_scenarios.scenario: Coordinate restoration across application, database, identity, and supplier teams while setting business priorities and executive updates.

practical_scenarios.title: Ticket backlog doubles after a portal redesign
practical_scenarios.scenario: Determine whether demand, form design, routing, knowledge, staffing, or hidden defects caused the increase.

practical_scenarios.title: A standard change causes repeated outages
practical_scenarios.scenario: Suspend or narrow pre-authorization, restore service, analyze why the standard model failed, and redesign criteria and controls.

practical_scenarios.title: Monitoring floods the NOC overnight
practical_scenarios.scenario: Reduce noise without suppressing meaningful risk and restore reliable on-call behavior.

practical_scenarios.title: Critical certificate expires in 48 hours
practical_scenarios.scenario: Coordinate renewal with incomplete ownership and uncertain dependency mapping.

practical_scenarios.title: Cloud cost rises 40 percent with no known project
practical_scenarios.scenario: Investigate cost allocation, demand, configuration drift, commitments, and possible misuse without making unsafe shutdowns.
preferred_response: Segment by account, service, tag, and unit

practical_scenarios.title: Users cannot access a system after an organizational restructure
practical_scenarios.scenario: Resolve accumulated mover-access issues while protecting segregation of duties.

practical_scenarios.title: Supplier reports green status while your customers fail
practical_scenarios.scenario: Establish end-to-end evidence and coordinate a multi-supplier incident.

practical_scenarios.title: CMDB shows the failed server as retired
practical_scenarios.scenario: Use alternate evidence for response and repair the data-governance failure afterward.
preferred_response: Verify cloud, network, monitoring, and owner data

practical_scenarios.title: Emergency patch requested during peak business hours
practical_scenarios.scenario: Balance active exploit risk, service impact, incomplete testing, rollback, and authorization.

practical_scenarios.title: Repeated incident is always closed as user error
practical_scenarios.scenario: Challenge categorization and perform evidence-based problem analysis.

practical_scenarios.title: Backup jobs succeed but restoration fails
practical_scenarios.scenario: Treat the issue as continuity failure and establish recoverability.
preferred_response: Identify missing data, keys, or dependencies
